whyItHolds.heading: The safety net is built in, not remembered
whyItHolds.paragraph1: The important rules — checking who's allowed to do what, never leaking a secret, protecting a payment — are enforced automatically. No one has to remember to add them, because there's no way to leave them out.
whyItHolds.paragraph2: If a piece isn't set up yet — no email account connected, no AI key added — nothing breaks. That one feature just waits quietly until you switch it on.

auth.title: Sign-in that's already done
auth.blurb: Email and password work on day one; OAuth and magic links turn on the moment you add keys.

kernel.title: A handler shape you can't get wrong
kernel.blurb: Every route and action declares its auth mode, its input schema, its rate limit — a raw handler fails lint by construction.

config.title: One registry, not a scattered process.env
config.blurb: Every env var is declared once — required, secret, what it enables — and the doctor, the docs, and the code can never disagree.

billing.title: Payments that unlock things
billing.blurb: Stripe checkout and webhooks, wired end to end — free mode when it's off, so nothing blocks a demo.

llm.title: An AI gateway, not a vendor lock-in
llm.blurb: Local, OpenRouter, or a direct key — swap providers without touching a single call site.

jobs.title: Cron your agent can trust
jobs.blurb: Cron, fan-out and per-step retries when they're on — and every on-demand run works exactly the same when they're off.

security.title: SSRF guarded, not just documented
security.blurb: A fetch of a user-supplied URL is scheme-checked, range-blocked, and re-validated after connect — see the refusal happen, not just read about it.

email.title: Email that never blocks a signup
email.blurb: Resend in production, the console in dev — nothing waits on a provider that isn't there.

observability.title: See it break before your users do
observability.blurb: Product analytics and error tracking, both a silent no-op when you haven't set them up yet.

auth.whatItDoesBody: From the caller's side: every session-gated route and server action gets a resolved, real session.user handed to it, or it never runs at all — there is no in-between state to handle.
auth.ruleBody: Auth mode is mandatory, with no default. Every defineAction call states auth: "required" or "public" explicitly — there is nowhere to omit the decision, so a public action can never accidentally ship without one.
auth.workingExampleBody: Auth is the one baseline that isn't optional — set BETTER_AUTH_SECRET and email/password sign-in works immediately; everything else here is an upgrade, not a requirement.
auth.ctaParagraph: Create an account, then open the dashboard — that's requireSession doing its job.

billing.whatItDoesBody: From a paywalled action's side: one call, getEntitlement(userId), answers "what is this user allowed today" — a plan id and a runsPerDay limit, whether billing is configured or not.
billing.ruleBody: getEntitlement() never talks to the billing provider directly — only the cached subscription row in Postgres — so a slow or down provider can never slow down or break a request that just needs to know a plan limit. With billing off, nothing is gated: every account gets the free plan's limit lifted entirely.

config.whatItDoesBody: From the caller's side: one function, getClientConfig(), boils down every service's runtime state into the small, safe slice of it a browser is ever allowed to see — a boolean per capability, nothing more.
config.ruleBody: The client boundary carries on/off booleans only. Adapter identities — which provider is actually behind "llm" or "email" — never cross it, because that's recon data for an attacker probing what a deployment runs. A component that needs to show "billing is on" can; nothing can ask "is it Stripe" from the browser.
config.realSourceIntro: The type this page's live capability map below is built from:
config.workingExampleIntro: Not a mockup — this is this deployment's own capability map, read at request time.

email.whatItDoesBody: From a caller's side: one send() call, naming a template and its typed props, works the same whether Resend is configured, missing, or you're in local dev — the caller never branches on which.
email.ruleBody: send() reads the email capability once and picks exactly one path — disabled, console, or Resend — and the Resend SDK is only ever imported on that last branch. A signup can never hang waiting on a provider that isn't configured; without one, it just quietly reports itself undelivered instead.
email.templatesIntro: Every template pairs its component with its subject line in one map, never scattered across call sites:
email.workingExampleIntro: No preview is rendered here — apps/web deliberately carries no dependency on @factory/email, so nothing outside the adapter package it belongs to can import the vendor renderer.
email.turnItOnBody: Set RESEND_API_KEY (and EMAIL_FROM) and delivery goes live. Leave it unset: in development every email prints to the console instead; in production, email is off entirely and sign-up just skips the verification step rather than blocking on it.

kernel.whatItDoesBody: From the caller's side: every route and server action in this repo declares its auth mode, its input schema, and (when public) its rate-limit policy up front, in one place, before any of your handler code runs.
kernel.ruleBody: defineHandler and defineAction are the ONLY legal way to declare a route handler or server action. A raw export async function GET/POST/..., or a raw exported function in a "use server" file, fails lint by construction — there is nowhere left to forget an auth check, skip input validation, or ship an unlimited public endpoint by accident.
kernel.realSourceIntro: The handler backing the live example below, declared the only legal way, next to the raw handler shape it replaces:
kernel.workingExampleBody: This calls the real echo endpoint above, on this deployment. It costs nothing, needs no account, and makes no outbound request — the handler only echoes a capped slice of what you send it.
kernel.asymmetryNote: One asymmetry worth noticing: the origin check above (defineHandler's step 4) only runs for state-changing methods, and it allows a request with no Origin header at all while rejecting one whose sec-fetch-site is cross-site. That means a copyable curl command succeeds against this route where a cross-origin browser call from another site is refused — the check targets the browser threat model (CSRF from a signed-in tab), not server-to-server callers, which is exactly why it works that way rather than being a hole in it.

llm.whatItDoesBody: From a caller's side: streamArray() takes a zod schema for ONE array element and hands your code a fully-typed element every time the model completes one — no partial objects, no vendor SDK types leaking out of @factory/llm.
llm.ruleBody: Every call — streaming or not — goes through the same budget check, cost accounting, and llm_calls row, whichever provider profile is configured (local, OpenRouter, or a direct key). A call site never spends money it wasn't told it could, and a disabled or over-budget call throws before any provider SDK is even loaded.
llm.turnItOnBody: Set credentials for any one profile and it lights up. Leave all of it unset and streamArray()/generate() throw before any provider SDK loads; every call site in this template is written to fall back to a non-AI result rather than let that throw reach a user.

observability.whatItDoesBody: From a caller's side: track() fires an analytics event and captureException() reports an error — both are unconditional calls you never wrap in a capability check yourself.
observability.ruleBody: Two independent seams under one banner: product analytics via PostHog and error tracking via Sentry, plus OpenTelemetry tracing underneath the LLM and job pipelines. Either can be on, off, or both — neither depends on the other, and neither depends on any other service in the template. track() is fire-and-forget by contract: it never blocks the caller and never throws, whether analytics is on, off, or the call itself fails.
observability.workingExampleBody: Set POSTHOG_KEY for analytics and/or SENTRY_DSN for error reporting — each lights up independently. Leave either unset and its functions become silent no-ops: no vendor SDK is ever imported, and nothing that calls track() or captureException() changes behavior.

security.whatItDoesBody: From a feature's side: any code that needs to fetch a URL the user supplied calls safeFetch() instead of the global fetch, and gets SSRF protection for free — no per-feature range-checking code to get wrong.
security.ruleBody: A user-supplied URL can point at a hostname that resolves safely at DNS-lookup time and somewhere internal (a cloud metadata endpoint, a private-network service) by the time the connection actually lands — DNS-rebinding. The rule safeFetch enforces is: never trust the pre-connect DNS answer. Validate the socket you actually got.

security.realSourceIntro2: The actual defense against DNS-rebinding is the post-connect check that calls this predicate against the real, connected socket, not the DNS answer:
security.workingExampleBody: isBlockedAddress takes an IP address literal, not a hostname — it fails closed (blocked) for anything that isn't a valid IPv4/IPv6 literal, which is why the field below takes an IP, not a URL. This is DNS-free: no lookup, no fetch is ever performed by this page.

index.heading: The machinery behind the product
index.argumentParagraph: The argument, end to end: what you get on day one, the rule that makes a shortcut impossible, proof it's enforced on this exact deployment, proof the product keeps working when a piece is missing, how to run it yourself, and every piece you can build on next.
index.liveHeading: Capability lights, not a marketing claim

index.builtHeading: Nine pieces, four of them load-bearing
index.builtBody: Auth, the kernel, config, and security ship unconditionally — there's no env var that turns them off. The rest are checked live against this deployment's own runtime, the same signal the control panel above reads.
